clue.text: Slightly scary counterpart back in Cyprus

indicators.note: the turned-round counterpart sits in the letters for Cyprus

parts.note: CY is the international code for Cyprus
a peer is an equal, a counterpart

explanation.surface: Someone's opposite number returning to Cyprus is a mildly unnerving prospect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Counterpart' reads as an opposite number in the surface, but it means an equal; CY is the international country code for Cyprus.
explanation.definitionFit: Creepy means somewhat frightening or unsettling.

clue.text: Champion golfer's yarn

definitions.meaning: the surname of Henry, three-time winner of the Open Championship
yarn here is spun thread, named by its plant fibre

explanation.surface: A golf champion spins a long story.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry Cotton was a British golfer who won the Open three times; 'yarn' wants to mean a tale but here it is thread.
explanation.definitionFit: Cotton is a golfer's surname and also a kind of thread or yarn.

clue.text: Special changes encompassing work of bishops

indicators.note: the rearranged SPECIAL wraps round the word for work
SPECIAL 'changes' its letter order

parts.note: OP is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: Particular reforms take in the business of a church's bishops.
explanation.walkthrough: OP for a musical or literary work is a standard abbreviation of opus.
explanation.definitionFit: Episcopal means relating to or governed by bishops.

clue.text: Saw senior scout in lead

indicators.note: the senior scout goes in the symbol for lead

parts.note: Pb is the chemical symbol for lead
a Rover Scout was an older member of the Scout movement

explanation.surface: An older scout spotted someone out in front.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' reads as the past tense of see, but it is the noun: an old saying. 'Lead' is the metal, not the front position.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw is a traditional saying, which is what a proverb is.

clue.text: Choose randomly from all the players, a great many

parts.note: the cast is everyone acting in a production

explanation.surface: A director picks at random from a large company of actors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Players' suggests a sports team, but it is the actors in a show.
explanation.definitionFit: To cast lots is to decide something by drawing or throwing lots, at random.

clue.text: Can we please fans winning everything?

indicators.note: to fan is to spread out, scattering the letters of the phrase before it

explanation.surface: A team asks how it can keep its supporters happy, and the answer is to win every game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fans' looks like the supporters in the surface, but it is the verb that spreads the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A clean sweep is a victory in every contest or category.

clue.text: Vessel left during high water, heading for Rotterdam

indicators.note: the left goes during, that is inside, the rearranged water
high means drunk, so WATER is reeling

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for left

indicators.note: the heading of Rotterdam is its first letter

explanation.surface: A ship departs at high tide, bound for the Dutch port of Rotterdam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High water' reads as high tide, but 'high' is a separate word meaning drunk that scrambles WATER.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain definition by category: the answer is one kind of vessel, a fishing boat that drags a net.

clue.text: Style of painting round Split?

explanation.surface: An art style found around the Croatian city of Split.
explanation.walkthrough: Split is capitalised to look like the Croatian port, but it is the verb part.
explanation.definitionFit: Op art is a 1960s style of painting built on optical illusions.

clue.text: Leave with group on Scottish river

parts.note: the Forth is the river that flows into the sea past Edinburgh

explanation.surface: A party departs together on a river in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' puts the group before the river in a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the phrasal verb means to depart, usually at the start of a journey.

clue.text: Expedition party turned back making stand

indicators.note: the party is turned to face backwards

explanation.surface: A group of explorers retreats and makes a stand against the odds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stand' suggests resistance, but it is the noun: a three-legged support.
explanation.definitionFit: A tripod is a three-legged stand for a camera or similar.

clue.text: Nice at Naples, at sea

indicators.note: letters at sea are adrift and out of place

explanation.surface: A trip from Nice on the French Riviera to Naples by boat.
explanation.walkthrough: Nice is capitalised only because it starts the clue; it is the adjective, not the French city.
explanation.definitionFit: Nice and pleasant both mean agreeable.

clue.text: Has rector upset band?

indicators.note: upset letters are knocked out of their order

explanation.surface: A vicar has been offended by a group of musicians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Band' looks like the thing that upset the rector, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: band means any group of musicians, and this is the large classical kind.

clue.text: Consider taking in second pub with editor quick to take offence

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second

explanation.surface: Think about going to another pub with an editor who is easily offended.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking in' applies only to the second, S, which goes inside THINK; the pub and editor follow on.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: a skin too thin to protect you stands for touchiness, so the phrase describes the easily offended.

clue.text: Bishop not participating in very tight game

indicators.note: the bishop takes no part in the word, so he is removed from it

parts.note: tight means drunk, and blotto means very drunk
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A bishop sits out a closely fought match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very tight' suggests a close contest, but tight is slang for drunk; blotto is very drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Lotto is a game of chance like bingo.

clue.text: Government employee cut verbal spin when broadcast

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered widely, so the letters are strewn about

explanation.surface: A civil servant trims the political spin in a speech before it goes on air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' wants to be the instruction to remove letters; it is just part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the phrase names anyone working for the state, the same thing as a civil servant.

clue.text: A storage tower erected to store produce in citadel

indicators.note: the A and the upturned silo hold the produce between them
in a down clue, erecting the tower sets it upside down, reading upwards

parts.note: a silo is a tower for storing grain

explanation.surface: A grain tower is put up to keep the harvest safe inside a fortress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Produce' reads as a verb but is the noun, crops.
explanation.definitionFit: An acropolis is the fortified citadel of an ancient Greek city.

clue.text: Medical material

definitions.meaning: as a noun, a medical is a check-up by a doctor
material as an adjective: made of matter, bodily

explanation.walkthrough: The two words look like a pair of adjectives, but 'Medical' is the noun for a check-up, which is also called a physical.
explanation.definitionFit: A physical is a medical examination, and physical means material, of the body or the world of matter.

clue.text: Slide headlong

definitions.meaning: a spiral slide at a fair
headlong means in reckless, disorderly haste

explanation.walkthrough: A helter-skelter is a spiral slide round a tower at a British fairground.
explanation.definitionFit: The fairground ride is a slide, and helter-skelter as an adverb means in headlong disorderly haste.

clue.text: Slip one prepared for Greek character

indicators.note: the letters are prepared, worked into a new form

explanation.surface: An actor lets a line slip, ready to play a Greek role.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' suggests a person in a play; it is a letter of the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Epsilon is the fifth letter of the Greek alphabet.

clue.text: Information sent over about old soldier

indicators.note: sending the information over flips it end to end

parts.note: a report is a piece of information
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: Intelligence is passed on concerning a veteran serviceman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old soldier' wants to be read together, but 'old' is the O and 'soldier' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A trooper is a private soldier, especially in the cavalry.

clue.text: Found shelter

definitions.meaning: to dig something out is to find it
a shelter here is a covered pit excavated in the ground, as in trenches

explanation.walkthrough: 'Found' looks like the verb that builds the shelter, but it means discovered.
explanation.definitionFit: Dug out means found after a search, and a dugout is a shelter dug into the ground.

clue.text: Small baked items for operatives

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: A tray of little pastries is laid on for the workers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Operatives' suggests factory workers; here it means secret agents.
explanation.definitionFit: A specialised sense: in intelligence work an operative is a secret agent.

clue.text: Turn of phrase in papers I'm carrying round

indicators.note: I'M carries the round letter inside it

explanation.surface: A writer spots a nice phrase in the newspapers they are carrying about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Papers' reads as newspapers, but it means identity documents, ID.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a turn of phrase is a fixed expression whose meaning is not the sum of its words.

clue.text: Unprepared, I'm put out about concert

indicators.note: PUT goes about the concert before being mixed
PUT is put out of its normal order

parts.note: a prom is a promenade concert, as at the BBC Proms in London

explanation.surface: A performer, caught cold, is annoyed about having to play a concert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out' reads as annoyed, but it is PUT plus an instruction to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Impromptu means done without preparation.

clue.text: Hold on tightly crossing short incline that's frightening

indicators.note: the hill is cut short by a letter
the word for hold on tightly lies across the shortened slope

parts.note: a verb meaning to grip fast
a hill is an incline; short drops its last letter

explanation.surface: Gripping hard while crossing a brief but scary slope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crossing' pictures walking over the slope, but here it means the grip word lies across the hill, one letter either side.
explanation.definitionFit: Something chilling is frightening, enough to make you go cold.

clue.text: American referendum over space programme

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for American
a referendum is a poll of voters
O is the cricket scoring abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: The US holds a vote on its space spending.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' reads as 'about', but it is O from cricket scorecards, where an over is a set of six balls.
explanation.definitionFit: Apollo was NASA's space programme that landed people on the Moon.

clue.text: French daily taking in a fizzy drink

indicators.note: the newspaper takes the A inside it

parts.note: Le Monde is a French daily newspaper

explanation.surface: Someone reads the Paris paper over a soft drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The A slips into LE MONDE between its N and D.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain lemonade is a fizzy lemon-flavoured soft drink.

clue.text: Happy days for model?

parts.note: pro means for, in favour of
to model for an artist is to sit

explanation.surface: Good times lie ahead for someone who models.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Happy days' reads as a pleasant spell, but it is a drinking toast, like cheers.
explanation.definitionFit: Prosit is a toast, like the British 'happy days!' said on raising a glass.
